items.exact_i_can: I can construct rate-of-change statements from tables, graphs, and situations.
items.learning_target: I can construct rate-of-change statements from tables, graphs, and situations.
items.student_html:
A student is tracking distance from a starting point during a steady walk. Study the graph before using any formal slope formula.

(a) Describe how the distance changes each minute. (b) Use two visible points to estimate how many blocks are added for each additional minute. (c) Predict the distance at 5 minutes and explain what feature of the graph makes that prediction reasonable.
items.student_text: A student is tracking distance from a starting point during a steady walk. Study the graph before using any formal slope formula. (a) Describe how the distance changes each minute. (b) Use two visible points to estimate how many blocks are added for each additional minute. (c) Predict the distance at 5 minutes and explain what feature of the graph makes that prediction reasonable.
items.answer_html: The distance increases by 3 blocks each minute. The graph has a constant rise/run of 3 blocks per minute. At 5 minutes the model gives 16 blocks; the straight-line pattern supports the prediction.
items.evidence_job: Preview constant rate as a measurable feature across a shared graph.
items.source_basis: Current Unit Assessment Plan + Algebra 1 Framework section enrichment + Toolkit WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01

items.learning_target: I can design linear models that represent patterns in real-world data.
items.student_html:
A student measures a plant once each week. The data do not fall on a perfect line.

(a) Describe the overall trend. (b) Sketch mentally where a reasonable straight trend line would run through the cloud of points. (c) Estimate the height at week 5 from the data pattern. (d) Explain why a useful model does not require every point to lie exactly on one line.
items.student_text: A student measures a plant once each week. The data do not fall on a perfect line. (a) Describe the overall trend. (b) Sketch mentally where a reasonable straight trend line would run through the cloud of points. (c) Estimate the height at week 5 from the data pattern. (d) Explain why a useful model does not require every point to lie exactly on one line.
items.answer_html: The data show a strong positive, roughly linear trend. A reasonable line would pass through the middle of the points. Around week 5 the height is about 14–15 cm. Real measurements vary, so a model summarizes the trend rather than matching every observation exactly.
items.evidence_job: Preview linear modeling as trend description rather than perfect fit.
